```{r setup, include=FALSE}
knitr::opts_chunk$set(collapse = TRUE, comment = "#>", fig.width = 6, fig.height = 4)
library(gof)
```

## Genuine ties enter one step

The cumulative process adds all residuals whose ordering coordinate is at most
the evaluation point. Observations at the same coordinate therefore enter
together. If two tied observations have residuals +1 and -1, their combined
jump is zero; there is no intermediate +1 step. Arbitrarily ordering them or
adding jitter would change the statistic.

The observations remain separate residual units. Tying their coordinates does
not assign them one common subject multiplier, drop rows or average away their
responses. The grouped step is also used for simulations. There is no random,
first/last or average-rank switch for this statistic.

The half-open moving window `(t-b, t]` matches Lin, Wei and Ying (2002),
equation (2.7); a closed window can differ at coincident entry/exit events.
For `"predicted"`, gof uses fitted response means, whereas that paper's
equation (2.10) uses fitted linear predictors. A strictly increasing transform
preserves the all-point cumulative Sup statistic, but generally changes the
L2 integration measure and fixed-bandwidth windows. These are specified
coordinate conventions, not interchangeable statistics. Supplying an
outcome-estimated predictor under an observed-variable name does not make it
a fixed ordering or establish its regularity.

## Declare an observed measurement resolution

By default, observed numeric ordering values are used as supplied. If the
recording convention supplies a meaningful resolution, declare it explicitly
before inspecting diagnostic results:

```{r declared-resolution}
set.seed(210)
d <- data.frame(x = seq(-1, 1, length.out = 80))
d$y <- rpois(nrow(d), exp(0.4 + 0.7 * d$x))
fit <- glm(y ~ x, data = d, family = poisson())

recorded <- fit |> cumres(
  variable = "x", resolution = c(x = 0.25), R = 39, plots = 0
)
recorded$ordering
as.data.frame(recorded)[, c("variable", "test", "statistic", "p.value",
                          "ordering_status", "resolution", "tie_blocks")]
```

The coordinate becomes `round(x / 0.25) * 0.25`. The grid origin is zero;
R rounds represented half-step values to the nearest even integer. Binary
representation can affect values near a rounding boundary. Choose an explicitly
transformed fixed variable yourself for other recording origins or bin rules.
No tolerance is inferred from the significance of the resulting test.

Only the diagnostic coordinate changes. The model retains its original
covariates, fit, offsets, residuals and independent units. `resolution` must
name selected observed numeric variables; it cannot target `"predicted"`.
Very fine steps whose integer grid indices exceed exact double representation
are rejected. Coarsening can change both power and the coordinate measure in
L2, so it is part of the diagnostic specification.

Response bootstrap uses the same declared fixed coordinate and grid for the
observation and every simulated sample:

```{r bootstrap-resolution}
set.seed(211)
bootstrap <- fit |> cumres_bootstrap(
  variable = "x", resolution = c(x = 0.25), R = 39, plots = 0
)
bootstrap$ordering
```

Fitted-null bootstrap remains approximate under its documented sampling and
estimation assumptions. Declaring resolution does not fix small-sample
calibration, model selection or a wrong sampling distribution.

## Fitted ordering has a separate numerical check

For `lm`/`glm`, predictions are reconstructed from coefficients and offsets,
so identical design/offset rows remain tied. Between different rows, fitting
error can split an exact tie, collapse distinct predictions or reverse their
order. Sup is particularly sensitive to an extra step between a split tie.

The default check uses a local Fisher-score correction, conditioning and
accumulated-roundoff allowances to screen adjacent fitted comparisons and
moving-window entry/exit events. A stable ordering of fitted values alone does
not settle their separation by bandwidth. The check consumes no random draws,
does not refit the model and does not modify fitted
coordinates. This is an ordinary local numerical diagnostic, **not** a formal
interval/root certificate, proof of exact ties, or guarantee that the
asymptotic/statistical calibration is valid. High-precision references are
development validation tools; users do not need a high-precision dependency.

```{r checked-ordering}
checked <- fit |> cumres(variable = c("predicted", "x"), R = 39, plots = 0)
checked$ordering[, c("variable", "source", "status", "reason")]
```

The `informative` score-space flag and the ordering precision status answer
different questions. A numerically stable coordinate need not contain useful
lack-of-fit information, and an observed score-space constraint does not
establish that fitted coordinates were computed accurately.

## Choose how unresolved ordering is reported

`on_unresolved = "report"` is the default. A flagged fitted ordering generates
a warning; its numerical curve/statistic remains available descriptively but
its inferential Sup/L2 p-values are missing. Other resolved marginal diagnostics
remain available. A joint family containing it withholds its entire family
inference and simultaneous envelope, without silently removing the member.

The following symmetric count totals have an exact flat fitted mean. The
example deliberately retains an ordinary finite-precision GLM fit:

```{r unresolved-ordering}
set.seed(7281)
flat_data <- data.frame(x = rep(c(-1, 0, 1), each = 100))
flat_data$y <- unlist(lapply(c(200, 187, 200), function(total) {
  drop(rmultinom(1, total, rep(0.01, 100)))
}))
flat_fit <- glm(y ~ x, data = flat_data, family = poisson(),
                control = glm.control(epsilon = 1e-12))

# Ordinary calls also warn. Suppress it here to display the returned reason.
flat <- suppressWarnings(cumres(flat_fit, variable = c("predicted", "x"),
                                R = 19, plots = 0))
flat$ordering[, c("variable", "status", "reason")]
as.data.frame(flat)[, c("variable", "test", "statistic", "p.value",
                       "ordering_status")]
```

Strict workflows can use `on_unresolved = "error"`. This stops before any
simulation, allowing a calling pipeline to handle the failure explicitly:

```{r strict-policy}
tryCatch(
  cumres(flat_fit, variable = "predicted", on_unresolved = "error",
         R = 19, plots = 0),
  error = function(e) conditionMessage(e)
)
```

Increasing optimizer precision can help, but a small deviance change alone
does not certify every fitted comparison. Rounding fitted values or trying
different policies until a preferred p-value appears is not a repair.
Prespecified fixed covariate ordering avoids this estimated-coordinate issue
while retaining its own sampling and calibration assumptions.

## Scope and recorded metadata

`resolution` supports `cumres.lm`/`cumres.glm`, their `cumres_joint` wrapper and
`cumres_bootstrap`. `on_unresolved` controls the linear/GLM fitted-order check;
it does not change bootstrap failure bounds or substitute for MLE-existence
checks. The controls are not implemented for ordinal/SEM adapters or arbitrary
explicit residual callbacks, which reject them rather than silently ignore them.

`object$ordering` records source, `ties = "group"`, declared resolution,
distinct coordinates, tied blocks/units, changed units, status and reason.
Units are those of the residual engine, including expanded binomial trials.
`object$ordering_check` stores local numerical details. Result tables, summaries
and optional tidy methods retain ordering availability. Objects saved without
this metadata retain the previous core result columns.

Fitted status is `"specified"` for no estimated coefficients, `"structural"`
for one natural-parameter cell, `"saturated"` for saturated natural-parameter
cells with the required precision structure, `"checked"` after other local
comparisons pass, or `"unresolved"`. Observed coordinates have status `"fixed"`.
A passed check does not generalize the supported inferential method.

In particular, fitted-order response bootstrap remains unsupported. Full
refitting/reordering alone does not solve the raw L2 random-range problem at
flat means. The existing response bootstrap uses prespecified fixed orderings.

## References and implementation boundaries

R's [empirical distribution function documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/ecdf.html)
illustrates grouped jumps at tied values. The weighted residual step follows
the same indicator convention.

The `survival` package's
[numerical controls](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/survival/html/coxph.control.html)
distinguish numerical tie repair from statistical tie methods, and warn that
automatic repair can merge genuine differences. gof does not borrow Cox tie
methods or automatically merge fitted values.

R's [glm.control documentation](https://stat.ethz.ch/R-manual/R-devel/library/stats/html/glm.control.html)
defines a deviance-based stopping criterion. The local gof screen is a
documented numerical implementation choice, independently checked against
high-precision and exact-rational development references; it is not a newly
claimed published hypothesis test. The original cumulative-residual method
and remaining inferential conditions are described in the statistical guide.
